name: Obedience and Conformity
what: This subtopic covers the psychological concepts of obedience and conformity, the factors that influence each, the landmark experiments by Milgram (1963) and Asch (1951), contemporary replications, and the ethical issues these studies raise.
why: Both obedience and conformity are present in everyday life and can lead people to act in ways they would not choose individually, ranging from following reasonable authority to participating in harm. Understanding the mechanisms behind them supports more critical thinking about one's own behaviour.

items.title: I can define obedience and identify three factors that increase its likelihood
items.what: Obedience is complying with commands from a perceived authority figure. The three main factors increasing obedience are: higher status or power of the authority figure, greater physical or relational proximity to that figure, and observing others obeying the same commands.
items.why: Knowing these factors helps explain why authority symbols such as uniforms, proximity, and social proof are so effective at producing compliance, and why people in positions of authority carry significant responsibility.
items.example: A student is more likely to sit down when instructed by a teacher standing right next to them (high proximity and high status) than when a classmate calls out the same instruction from across the room (low status, low proximity).

items.title: I can describe the aim, procedure, and results of Milgram's (1963) obedience experiment
items.what: Milgram aimed to test how far 40 male participants would obey an experimenter's instructions to administer electric shocks of increasing voltage to a confederate acting as a learner. Despite visible distress in many participants, 65% (26 of 40) continued to the maximum 450 volts.
items.why: The results were far higher than any expert predicted beforehand, demonstrating that ordinary people can cause serious harm to others when instructed by a perceived authority, a finding with direct relevance to understanding atrocities like the Holocaust.
items.example: Before the study, 14 Yale psychology students predicted on average that only about 1.2% of participants would administer the maximum shock. The actual result was 65%, showing how dramatically humans underestimate the power of authority.

items.title: I can evaluate Milgram's experiment against at least two ethical guidelines
items.what: Milgram's experiment breached three key ethical standards: the no-harm principle (participants experienced psychological distress and a 45-volt real shock), withdrawal rights (participants were told to continue despite wanting to leave), and informed consent/debriefing (participants were deceived about the study's true purpose).
items.why: Evaluating studies against ethical guidelines is a required skill in VCE Psychology and reflects the broader principle that scientific value does not justify causing lasting harm to participants.
items.example: When participants verbally said they wanted to stop, the experimenter responded with scripted phrases such as 'the experiment requires you continue,' which pressured them to stay despite their right to withdraw without penalty.

items.title: I can describe the key findings of Caspar et al. (2016) and explain what they add to our understanding of obedience
items.what: Caspar et al. found that when participants were ordered to press a key that delivered a mild shock, they perceived their action as more passive than when they chose freely, suggesting that being ordered to act reduces a person's felt sense of responsibility and agency.
items.why: This study updates Milgram's findings using ethical methods with genuine informed consent. It suggests that obedience works partly by allowing people to psychologically distance themselves from the consequences of their actions.
items.example: In the study, participants judged the time between pressing a key and hearing a tone as longer when ordered than when choosing freely, indicating their actions felt less like their own when commanded, even when no harm was caused.

items.title: I can define conformity and identify four factors that influence it
items.what: Conformity is adjusting thoughts, feelings, or behaviours to match those of others, a social group, or a social situation. Four factors that increase conformity are: social norms, groupthink, group shift, and deindividuation.
items.why: Conformity is often invisible in everyday life because it feels natural, yet it can lead individuals to behave in ways they later regret or find inconsistent with their values, as seen in bystander inaction and online bullying.
items.example: At a crowded public pool where nobody else is responding to a person in distress, an individual may conform to the group's inaction due to deindividuation, feeling neither visible nor personally responsible for helping.

items.title: I can describe the aim, procedure, and results of Asch's (1951) conformity experiment
items.what: Asch had 50 male university students complete a line-matching task in groups where all other members were confederates instructed to give a unanimously incorrect answer on 12 of 18 trials. Of the real participants, 74% conformed to at least one wrong answer, while 24% never conformed.
items.why: Asch's results show that social pressure is powerful enough to make people doubt clear perceptual evidence, demonstrating that conformity is driven more by the discomfort of standing out than by any genuine uncertainty about the correct answer.
items.example: Even participants who never conformed reported feeling confused and doubting their own correct answers during the study, showing that the pressure to conform was felt by everyone, not just those who gave in to it.

items.title: I can compare obedience and conformity using their key similarities and differences
items.what: Both obedience and conformity influence individual behaviour and occur in everyday life. The key difference is that obedience involves a direct command from an authority figure with punishment as the consequence of refusal, whereas conformity involves indirect social pressure from a group with social rejection as the consequence of non-compliance.
items.why: Distinguishing the two concepts is necessary for correctly identifying which mechanism is operating in a given scenario, an exam skill that requires careful attention to whether a direct command or indirect group pressure is driving the behaviour.
items.example: A student who sits down because a teacher tells them to is demonstrating obedience. The same student sitting down because everyone else in the class already has, without being told to, is demonstrating conformity.

items.title: I can describe Sun and Yu's (2016) conformity study and explain what it shows about the age at which conformity emerges
items.what: Sun and Yu showed kindergarten children a photo of a face, had them rate its attractiveness, then showed them fake peer ratings before asking them to rate again. Children around age six tended to shift their ratings toward the group's rating, while younger children did not.
items.why: This finding extends the relevance of Asch's research to young children and suggests that conformity to peer influence develops around age six, which has implications for education and understanding social development.
items.example: A five-year-old who rated a face as 4 out of 8 was unlikely to change their rating after seeing peers rate it as 6, whereas a six-year-old in the same situation was likely to revise their rating upward to match the group.
